# Applying a manifest to a running deployment

`rimsky compose` reconciles a running deployment against a declaration: plan the
change, compare against what is there, apply it, and tear it all down with one
command. Every resource the manifest creates carries the project's own prefix.

## The manifest

`rimsky-compose.yml`:

```yaml
project: lifecycle-demo
templates:
  - path: ./template-a.yml
    tag: alpha@1
    state: deployed
  - path: ./template-b.yml
    tag: beta@1
    state: deployed
instances:
  - template: alpha@1
    name: one
  - template: beta@1
    name: two
```

`template-a.yml`:

```yaml
name: manifest-node-a
version: "1"
message_queue_mode: backlog
nodes:
  - type: verify
    executor: verifier-shape-checks
    attributes:
      schema:
        type: object
        properties:
          checks:
            type: array
            default:
              - kind: no_nulls
                config:
                  fields: [id]
                severity: error
          rows:
            type: array
            default:
              - id: 1
```

## See what would change

```bash
rimsky compose plan -f rimsky-compose.yml
```

The plan lists all eight steps before any of the resources exist — register,
deploy, tag, create instance — and names the namespaced identities it would
create: `compose:lifecycle-demo:alpha@1`, `compose:lifecycle-demo:one`.

An operator reads the whole change as a list before committing to it, which is
what makes a multi-resource manifest safe to apply to a deployment that already
has work on it.

## Compare against the deployment

```bash
rimsky compose status -f rimsky-compose.yml
```

Before the apply, every declared resource reads `manifest-missing-from-api`.
After it, all four read `in-manifest`. The verb answers the drift question
without applying anything.

## Apply

```bash
rimsky compose up -f rimsky-compose.yml --yes
```

The eight steps run and the verb reports `applied`. Afterwards:

```bash
rimsky ls tags -o json
rimsky ls instances -o json
rimsky ls templates -o json
```

The tag, template and instance listings carry the `compose:lifecycle-demo:`
prefix on every resource the manifest created, and the templates read
`deployed`.

## Apply again

```bash
rimsky compose up -f rimsky-compose.yml --yes
# no changes
```

The second apply reports no changes rather than re-creating anything. The verb
drives the deployment towards the declaration instead of replaying a script, so
an operator can run the same command after an edit and get only the difference.

## Namespacing

Every resource the manifest owns is prefixed with `compose:<project>:`. An
operator sharing a deployment between a manifest and hand-authored work tells at
a glance which resources the manifest owns — which is what makes the
one-command teardown safe to run.

## Tear it down

`compose down` refuses to abort live instances, so drive them terminal first:

```bash
rimsky instance kill compose:lifecycle-demo:one --yes
rimsky instance kill compose:lifecycle-demo:two --yes

rimsky compose down -f rimsky-compose.yml --yes
# compose down complete
```

One command removes instances, deployments, tags and templates in eight steps,
and both listings come back clean. The teardown covers every kind of resource
the manifest declares.

## Posture

The compose verbs send no credential. They work on a deployment in the shipped
default posture, with no keys minted. On a deployment with authentication
enabled they fail unauthorized under every key-passing mechanism the CLI offers,
while an ordinary verb with the same key succeeds.
